## Challenge

We need to...

1. define the costs and benefits of each strategy and
2. explain why individuals would choose one strategy over another. 

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
To that end, we will develop a [**formal equilibrium model**]{.underline},
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
i.e., we will apply [**neoclassical orthodoxy**]{.underline}. [\[cue Wilhelm scream\]]{.text-mono .text-muted}
:::

## Economy

We assume an agrarian subsistence economy in which...

1. there is no trade or migration [(the economy is isolated)]{.text-muted},
2. production occurs on farms privately held by households, 
3. factors are limited to labor [(a variable input)]{.text-muted} and land [(a fixed input)]{.text-muted}, and
4. competition is perfect [(everyone is a price-*taker*)]{.text-muted}.

## Production

The energetic output of an individual farm is given by...

::: {.r-stack}
![](figures/production-0-axes.svg)

![](figures/production-1-total.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}

![](figures/production-2-average.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}

![](figures/production-3-marginal.svg){.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
:::

## Utility

We assign to each farm a time budget, $T$, and assume that they are utility
maximizers:

::: {style="margin: 2em 1em;"}

|            |                                                               |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Clients:   | $\max U_{c} = f(T-L) + wL \quad\;\; \text{s.t.}\;\; L \leq T$ |
| Patrons:   | $\max U_{p} = f(T+L) - wL$                                    |
: {.eq-table}

:::

where $w$ is the market wage and $L$ is time invested in wage-labor.

::: {.fragment .fade-in .min-callout-note style="margin-top: 2em"}
{{< iconify pixel:lightbulb >}} [note:]{.title} When $L = 0$, production reduces 
to pure subsistence, $f(T)$, in which case, there are no patrons or clients.
:::

## Supply

|            |                                                               |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Clients:   | $\max U_{c} = f(T-L) + wL \quad\;\; \text{s.t.}\;\; L \leq T$ |
: {.eq-table}

::: {.r-stack}
![](figures/supply-0-axes.svg)

![](figures/supply-1-subsistence.svg){.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5}
Total supply $S(w)$ is sum of $L^*$ for all client farms.
:::

|            |                            |

:::


## Competition

Market frictions...

![](figures/friction.svg)

If [A]{.text-mono} is sufficiently far, then competition between [A]{.text-mono} 
and [B]{.text-mono} for the household's labor will be imperfect, as [B]{.text-mono} 
will be able to set wages.

::: {.fragment .fade-in .min-callout-note style="margin-top: 1em"}
{{< iconify pixel:lightbulb >}} [note:]{.title} Failures of perfect competition 
in the Neolithic - notably the potential for monopsony power - is where we 
should look for the origins of inequality.
:::

## Conclusion

On this simple application of the neoclassical labor market model...

### STRENGTHS

- Orthodox: [Nothing in this should surprise an economist - it's econ 101.]{.text-muted}  
- Darwinian: [There's no collective action or group selection anywhere.]{.text-muted}  
- Unifying: [Many ideas about inequality can be absorbed into this model.]{.text-muted}
- Simple: [Promotes economy of thought, *contra* post-modernism.]{.text-muted}  

### WEAKNESSES, maybe

- Apolitical: [As presented, the model is largely silent about institutions, but that doesn't mean it has nothing to say about them!]{.text-muted}  
- Static: [The model does not account for population dynamics and changes in climate over time, but we can use it to do comparative statics!]{.text-muted}
